{{Short description|Mathematical conjecture}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Quillen–Lichtenbaum conjecture''' is a [[conjecture]] relating [[étale cohomology]] to [[algebraic K-theory]] introduced by {{harvtxt|Quillen|1975|p=175}}, who was inspired by earlier conjectures of {{harvtxt|Lichtenbaum|1973}}. {{harvtxt|Kahn|1997}} and {{harvtxt|Rognes|Weibel|2000}} [[mathematical proof|proved]] the Quillen–Lichtenbaum conjecture at the [[prime number|prime]] 2 for some [[number field]]s. [[Voevodsky]], using some important results of [[Markus Rost]], proved the [[Bloch–Kato conjecture]], which implies the Quillen–Lichtenbaum conjecture for all primes.

==Statement==

The conjecture in Quillen's original form states that if ''A'' is a finitely-generated algebra over the integers and ''l'' is prime, then there is a spectral sequence analogous to the [[Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequence]], starting at

:<math>E_2^{pq} = H^p_{\text{etale}}(\text{Spec }A[\ell^{-1}], Z_\ell(-q/2)),</math>  (which is understood to be 0 if ''q'' is [[parity (mathematics)|odd]])

and abutting to

:<math>K_{-p-q}A\otimes Z_\ell</math>

for −''p''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''q''&nbsp;>&nbsp;1&nbsp;+&nbsp;dim&nbsp;''A''.

==''K''-theory of the integers==
Assuming the  Quillen–Lichtenbaum conjecture and the [[Vandiver conjecture]], the ''K''-groups of the integers, ''K''<sub>''n''</sub>('''Z'''), are given by:

*0 if ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 mod 8 and ''n''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0, '''Z''' if ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0
*'''Z'''&nbsp;⊕&nbsp;'''Z'''/2 if ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 mod 8 and ''n''&nbsp;>&nbsp;1, '''Z'''/2 if ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1.
*'''Z'''/''c''<sub>''k''</sub> ⊕ '''Z'''/2 if ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2 mod&nbsp;8
*'''Z'''/8''d''<sub>''k''</sub> if ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3 mod 8
*0 if ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;4 mod 8
*'''Z''' if ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;5 mod 8
*'''Z'''/''c''<sub>''k''</sub> if ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;6 mod 8
*'''Z'''/4''d''<sub>''k''</sub> if ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;7 mod 8

where ''c''<sub>''k''</sub>/''d''<sub>''k''</sub> is the [[Bernoulli number]] ''B''<sub>2''k''</sub>/''k'' in lowest terms and ''n'' is 4''k''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 or 4''k''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;2 {{harv|Weibel|2005}}.
